screens.title: Upgradeable Contracts and Proxies
screens.subtitle: How to evolve logic while preserving state and address

narration.text: Smart contracts deployed to Ethereum are immutable. That immutable guarantee is powerful for security, but it creates a real maintenance problem when a bug appears or a new feature is needed. In this lesson you will learn a practical pattern that many teams use: separate the contract's state from its logic so the logic can be replaced while the state and address stay the same. The stable piece is called a proxy and the replaceable piece is the implementation or logic contract. The low-level operation that makes this work is delegatecall, which runs implementation code but uses the proxy's storage and original caller. We'll step through a minimal proxy example, show a deploy-and-upgrade lifecycle, and highlight the critical risks you must manage—especially storage collisions and initializer safety. By the end you will understand why upgradeability exists, when it is appropriate, and which controls are essential to keep upgrades safe. Consider whether your dApp really needs upgradeability or whether immutability is a better safety trade-off.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use a fixed proxy that holds state and forwards execution to changeable implementation contracts via delegatecall, preserving address and state across upgrades.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Upgradeable Contracts

Upgradeable Contracts and Proxies

Learn why immutability creates a maintenance challenge and how proxy patterns let you upgrade logic without losing state or changing the contract address.

Problem
Deployed code cannot change; bugs or feature needs require preserving state across upgrades.
Solution
Proxy + implementation split. Proxy holds state at a fixed address and forwards calls to changeable logic contracts.
Critical
delegatecall executes implementation code in the proxy's storage and preserves msg.sender for calls.
Risks
Storage collisions, initializer mistakes, and insecure upgrade control can break a contract irreparably.
Explore Key Topics
Proxy vs Implementation
Distinguish which contract keeps state and which provides logic.
The role of delegatecall
Why delegatecall preserves storage and original caller context.
Storage safety
How mismatched layouts produce collisions and how to avoid them.
Visual Concept
Proxy forwards to Implementation

A stable proxy address holds storage slots. The implementation pointer changes to upgrade logic while stored data remains intact.

Proxy
Quick Note
Always plan storage layout and protect initializer and upgrade functions. Prefer audited libraries for production systems.

screens.title: Immutability: problem and motivation
screens.subtitle: Why immutability drives the need for upgradeable patterns

narration.text: Immutability means once a smart contract is deployed, its bytecode cannot change. That immutability is a foundational security property: anyone can audit deployed code and trust it will behave the same forever. However, that same guarantee becomes a liability when a bug is discovered or new capabilities are required. Redeploying a corrected contract produces a new address and leaves all prior state behind. For many live applications, user balances, mappings, and integrations depend on the original address and stored data. Upgradeable contracts address this tension by separating state from logic. A stable proxy contract retains state at a fixed address while delegating execution to an implementation contract that can be swapped. Concretely, imagine a token with millions of users and a critical arithmetic bug. Without upgradeability you must advise every user to move tokens to a new contract, coordinate migrations, and update dozens of integrations. With a proxy you can deploy a fixed, well-protected proxy once and upgrade its implementation to fix the bug while user balances remain intact. A common misconception is that upgradeability eliminates audit needs; it doesn't. It shifts the audit surface: you must now audit proxy mechanics, storage layout, and upgrade controls. Think about whether the operational complexity of upgrades is justified compared to the safety of immutability.

keyIdea.title: Why upgradeability
keyIdea.text: Immutability protects users but prevents fixes; proxies let you evolve logic without losing state or changing address.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Immutability
Definition

Immutability: deployed contracts cannot change code. This guarantees consistent behavior but blocks post-deployment fixes.

Concrete example
A live token with a discovered arithmetic bug. Redeploying loses balances and breaks integrations; upgradeability preserves balances.
Misconception
Upgradeability removes the need for audits. Reality: it requires additional audits of proxy behavior and storage layout compatibility.
Key Takeaway

Immutability is both a feature and a constraint. Use upgradeability only when preserving state is essential and you can manage added complexity.

Contrast: Redeploy vs Upgrade
  • Redeploy: new address, lost state, migrations needed.
  • Upgrade: same address, preserved state, added indirection and governance required.
Decide based on user impact, frequency of changes, and your ability to secure upgrade procedures.

screens.title: Proxy and Implementation roles
screens.subtitle: How state and logic are separated in upgradeable patterns

narration.text: Upgradeable contracts split responsibilities across two contracts. The proxy is the stable on-chain address that holds the storage layout — variables, mappings, and balances — and it also typically contains the pointer to the implementation and the upgrade control logic. The implementation contract contains the business logic but does not manage persistent state itself; it expects to be executed in the proxy's storage. The crucial behavioral contract here is that when the proxy delegates a call, the implementation's code executes as if it were part of the proxy, so reads and writes happen against the proxy's storage. A clear example: a proxy stores a counter variable and an implementation provides an increment function. Users always call the proxy address. The proxy's fallback forwards the call and the increment logic updates the counter stored in the proxy. A common misconception is to interact directly with the implementation after deployment. Doing so initializes its own ephemeral storage or reveals uninitialized state. Always call through the proxy for user interactions. Architect your system so the proxy's storage layout is defined and frozen, and the implementation contracts are replaceable modules that adhere to that layout.

keyIdea.title: Role split
keyIdea.text: Proxy = storage and pointer; Implementation = logic executed in proxy's storage context via delegatecall.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Proxy vs Implementation
Proxy (Stable)
  • Holds persistent storage: variables and mappings.
  • Contains an implementation pointer and upgrade control.
  • Users interact exclusively with the proxy address.
Example scenario
Proxy stores a counter. Implementation exposes increment. Calls to increment go to the proxy and update proxy storage via delegatecall.
Implementation (Replaceable)
  • Contains business logic functions like increment, decrement, or transfer validation.
  • Should avoid constructors that initialize state — use initializer functions instead.
  • Can be redeployed and pointed to by the proxy when upgrading.
Pitfall
Interacting directly with the implementation after deployment can give misleading behavior because its storage is not the proxy's. Always perform state initialization and user calls through the proxy.
Practical reminder
Design storage layout in the proxy and treat implementations as stateless logic modules that must conform to that layout.

screens.title: delegatecall: semantics that make proxies work
screens.subtitle: What delegatecall does and why msg.sender and storage are preserved

narration.text: Delegatecall is the EVM opcode at the heart of proxy patterns. When a contract executes delegatecall to another address, the code at that address runs, but crucially the storage, the execution context, and the original caller remain those of the calling contract. That means the implementation's functions act on the proxy's storage slots, and msg. sender inside the implementation refers to the external account that called the proxy. This behavior is different from a normal call where the callee's storage and caller context belong to the callee contract. A concrete example from our sample flow: the proxy receives a call to increment, it delegatecalls the implementation's increment function, and the implementation increments the counter variable — but the counter slot being modified lives in the proxy. A common misconception is that delegatecall makes the implementation own the state. It does not; the proxy's storage is used. Because delegatecall uses the calling contract's storage layout, any mismatch between the implementation's expected layout and the proxy's actual layout can produce incorrect writes or overwrite critical proxy variables like the implementation pointer. That is why storage layout discipline and tooling to enforce compatibility are central to safe upgradeability.

keyIdea.title: Delegatecall essence
keyIdea.text: Delegatecall executes target code but uses the caller's storage and preserves the original msg.sender and msg.value.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › delegatecall
What delegatecall does
  • Executes code at the target address.
  • Uses the calling contract's storage slots for reads and writes.
  • Preserves msg.sender and msg.value from the original external caller.
Concrete example
Proxy receives increment call. It delegatecalls implementation. Implementation increases counter, and the counter in proxy storage changes.
Contrast: call vs delegatecall
call: callee uses its own storage and msg.sender is the caller contract.
delegatecall: callee's code runs but uses caller storage; msg.sender remains the original external caller.
Danger
Storage layout mismatch causes writes to unexpected slots and can corrupt proxy state or the implementation pointer itself.

screens.title: Minimal proxy and logic example
screens.subtitle: Understand the sample contracts and the fallback delegatecall flow

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal example that appears in the chapter. There are two logic contracts and a simple proxy. The logic contract defines a public numeric variable such as value or counter and exposes functions like initialize and increment. The logic contract intentionally avoids a constructor because constructors initialize the contract's own storage, not the proxy's. Instead, it provides an initializer function that the proxy calls once to set initial state. The proxy stores the implementation address and an owner. Its fallback function performs a delegatecall to the current implementation with the original calldata, so the implementation's code executes using the proxy storage and the original caller remains intact. A concrete flow: deploy LogicV1, deploy Proxy pointing at LogicV1, call initialize through the proxy to set the counter, call increment through the proxy and observe the proxy's counter increase, then deploy LogicV2, call upgradeTo on the proxy and subsequent calls run LogicV2 but still modify the proxy's storage. A common mistake is putting state variables in the implementation without aligning slots with the proxy; this is the source of storage collisions. Always initialize through the proxy and avoid interacting directly with implementation contracts for user flows.

keyIdea.title: Code pattern
keyIdea.text: Logic contracts provide functions and an initialize method; proxy stores state and uses a fallback that delegatecalls the implementation.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Minimal Example
Logic Contract (excerpt)
// Simplified logic contract
contract LogicV1 {
  uint public counter;

  function initialize(uint _initialValue) public {
    counter = _initialValue;
  }

  function increment() public {
    counter++;
  }

  function getVersion() public pure returns (string memory) {
    return "V1";
  }
}
Note: constructors are avoided in logic contracts so initialization happens in the proxy's storage context.
Proxy (excerpt)
contract SimpleProxy {
  address public implementation;
  address public owner;

  constructor(address _impl) {
    implementation = _impl;
    owner = msg.sender;
  }

  fallback() external payable {
    (bool success, bytes memory data) = implementation.delegatecall(msg.data);
    // return or revert with returned data
  }
}
The fallback forwards calldata to the implementation and returns the implementation's response to the original caller.
Key Takeaway

Always initialize and call through the proxy so state lives in the proxy and logic can be upgraded safely.

screens.title: Deploy and upgrade lifecycle
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step conceptual test of upgrading logic while preserving state

narration.text: Understanding the deploy-and-upgrade lifecycle is essential for testing upgradeability. Start by deploying your first logic contract, LogicV1. Next deploy a proxy and point it to LogicV1. Then call the initialize function through the proxy; this writes initial values into the proxy's storage. Exercise the implementation by calling functions like increment through the proxy and confirm state changes. To upgrade, deploy LogicV2 and run any required initialization steps through the proxy if needed. Then call the proxy's upgrade function, typically guarded by an owner or multisig, to set the implementation pointer to LogicV2. After the upgrade, calls to the proxy execute LogicV2 code but continue to read and write the proxy's storage. The chapter's hands-on steps illustrate this exact sequence. A common mistake is to skip calling initialize through the proxy; that leaves proxy storage uninitialized and can lead to unexpected values. Another pitfall is not simulating rollbacks or failure modes: always simulate failed upgrades to see how your governance and recovery controls behave. Testing upgrade flows conceptually helps you verify that state is preserved and that new functions behave as expected before any production deployment.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle steps
keyIdea.text: Deploy logic, deploy proxy pointing at logic, initialize via proxy, exercise functions, deploy new logic, upgrade proxy pointer, verify state and new behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Deploy & Upgrade Flow
Conceptual Steps
1. Deploy LogicV1
Prepare logic code and deploy the implementation contract.
2. Deploy Proxy
Proxy constructor points at LogicV1 and sets the owner who controls upgrades.
3. Initialize via Proxy
Call initialize through proxy so state is set in proxy storage.
4. Exercise Functions
Call increment or other functions to confirm behavior and state.
5. Upgrade
Deploy LogicV2, call upgradeTo on proxy, then test again to confirm state persists.
Example Check
After upgrade, getVersion through proxy should return the new version string while the counter value remains unchanged except for subsequent function calls.
Common mistake
Calling initialize on the implementation directly leaves proxy storage uninitialized and can corrupt expectations.

screens.title: Storage collisions — the silent hazard
screens.subtitle: How mismatched variable layouts corrupt proxy storage

narration.text: Storage collisions are the most subtle and dangerous risk when upgrading logic. They occur because delegatecall causes the implementation's code to read and write the proxy's storage slots. Solidity assigns storage slots deterministically based on the declared state variables and their order. If LogicV1 declares a single unsigned integer named value and LogicV2 later inserts a new address variable before value, the new address will occupy the same storage slot that previously held some other important proxy data. The practical consequence can be catastrophic: an added admin address in the implementation might overwrite the proxy's implementation pointer or owner variable, allowing malicious or accidental overwrites of upgrade control. A concrete illustration: LogicV1 had a first slot for implementation pointer in the proxy and the second slot for value in proxy storage. If LogicV2 shifts or adds variables, the code will access wrong slots. To avoid this, follow strict storage patterns: reserve fixed slots for proxy bookkeeping, use unstructured storage or fixed slot patterns for critical variables, and prefer upgrade libraries that enforce layout compatibility. A common misconception is that only new variables matter; in reality, changing order or type of any state variable can change slot assignment. Always check storage layout compatibility when releasing a new implementation.

keyIdea.title: Storage collision risk
keyIdea.text: delegatecall makes layout mismatches dangerous: variable order and types determine slots, and changes can overwrite proxy-critical data.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Storage Collisions
Why slot positions matter
Solidity assigns storage slots by variable declaration order and type. delegatecall makes implementation expect its own layout but operate on proxy storage. Any change in order or type shifts slots and can corrupt data.
Real consequence
A new variable in LogicV2 can overwrite the proxy's implementation or owner pointer, breaking upgrade controls or allowing takeover.
Prevention strategies
  • Reserve explicit slots for proxy bookkeeping using fixed storage slots.
  • Use unstructured storage patterns or storage gap arrays to allow future additions without reordering.
  • Prefer audited upgrade libraries that check layout compatibility when upgrading.
Misconception
Adding a harmless-looking variable is safe. Not true — even small changes can shift slot indices and cause corruption.
Key Takeaway

Plan storage layout carefully. Treat storage compatibility as a first-class part of upgrade design and testing.

screens.title: Initializer functions and constructor pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Why implementations use initializers and how to protect them

narration.text: Implementation contracts typically avoid constructors because constructors initialize the implementation contract's own storage, which is not used by the proxy. Instead, implementations provide initializer functions that the proxy calls once to populate proxy storage. An initializer acts like a constructor but must be guarded so it cannot be called more than once. Without protection an attacker or an accidental sequence could reinitialize state, resetting admin addresses or balances. In practice teams use an initializer modifier pattern that records whether initialization has run and prevents subsequent calls. A concrete example: LogicV1 exposes initialize that sets a counter to ten; the deployer calls initialize through the proxy immediately after proxy deployment. If LogicV2 also provides initialize but isn't protected, calling it after an upgrade could overwrite state unintentionally. A common misconception is that calling initialize directly on the implementation is equivalent; it is not. Calling initialize on the implementation affects the implementation's storage, not the proxy's. Always call initialize via the proxy to set proxy storage and protect initializer functions with an initializer modifier or equivalent guard. This practice preserves state integrity across deploys and upgrades.

keyIdea.title: Initializer safety
keyIdea.text: Use guarded initializer functions called through the proxy to set proxy state; never rely on constructors in implementation contracts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Initializer Functions
Why no constructors
Constructors run on the implementation's own deployment and set implementation storage. Since proxy storage is authoritative for user data, initial state must be set via a function called through the proxy.
Best practice
Use an initializer modifier to ensure the initializer can only be executed once for the proxy.
Common pitfalls
  • Initializing the implementation directly instead of via the proxy.
  • Forgetting to guard initialize, allowing re-initialization after upgrade.
  • Calling initialize twice across upgrades without handling already-initialized state.
Concrete check
After deploy, call initialize through the proxy and assert state values. After an upgrade, verify initialize cannot be abused to reset critical state.

screens.title: Upgrade mechanism security
screens.subtitle: Who can call upgradeTo and how to manage governance

narration.text: The upgrade mechanism is a high-power control point and must be guarded carefully. In the simple proxy example upgradeTo is restricted to the owner address, but that single-owner pattern concentrates power and risk. Best practice is to use an immutable governance control such as a multisig wallet or a time-locked multisig that requires multiple parties to sign off on upgrades and provides a delay for community review. The upgrade function should check the caller identity and perform minimal validation. When designing governance, include emergency and rollback procedures, and ensure upgrade actions are observable on-chain so users can monitor upcoming changes. A concrete governance flow: upgrades are proposed off-chain, reviewed and audited, and then a multisig executes the upgrade transaction after a public notice period. A common misconception is that upgrade authorization alone is sufficient; it isn't. You also need audit, staging, and simulation of upgrades to confirm storage compatibility. Treat upgradeTo as a scarce capability and design it to require multiple safeguards, testing, and transparent processes. Upgrade mechanism security means treat upgrade control as a scarce, audited capability. prefer multisig and staged upgrades with monitoring delays to reduce risk.. In practical terms, who can call upgradeto and how to manage governance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Governance
keyIdea.text: Treat upgrade control as a scarce, audited capability. Prefer multisig and staged upgrades with monitoring delays to reduce risk.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Upgrade Security
Hardening the upgrade path
Access control
Require multisig or timelock, avoid single-owner control where possible.
Review and audit
Audit new implementations and review storage layout changes before upgrade.
Staging and simulation
Simulate upgrades on testnets and confirm state preservation and failure handling.
Transparency
Announce upgrades and provide a delay to allow user and integrator readiness.
Concrete policy
Require at least two authorized signatures and a time delay for upgrade execution. Test rollback paths and publicize upgrade windows to users.

screens.title: Testing and auditing upgrade flows
screens.subtitle: Essential verification steps before a production upgrade

narration.text: Upgradeable systems add complexity that requires disciplined testing and auditing. Treat upgradeability as a multi-step verification process: first write unit tests that exercise all functions through the proxy, confirming state reads and writes behave as intended. Second, run integration tests that simulate the deploy-and-upgrade lifecycle: deploy LogicV1 and proxy, initialize via proxy, perform state changes, deploy LogicV2, execute upgrade, and verify state is maintained while new functionality works. Third, run negative tests and failure simulations: what happens if upgradeTo reverts, or if an initializer is called twice, or if an upgrade introduces a revert path for an existing function? Fourth, perform an audit focused on storage layout, delegatecall usage, and upgrade access controls. The chapter advises using battle-tested libraries such as those from reputable sources to reduce subtle bugs in the proxy mechanics. A common misconception is that passing unit tests alone is sufficient; you also need upgrade-specific simulations and security review focused on the indirection layer. Finally, include a rollback and emergency plan so you can respond if an upgrade results in unexpected behavior. Testing and auditing upgrade flows means test through the proxy, simulate upgrades and failures, and get storage-layout-focused audits before production upgrades.. In practical terms, essential verification steps before a production upgrade. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verification
keyIdea.text: Test through the proxy, simulate upgrades and failures, and get storage-layout-focused audits before production upgrades.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Testing & Audit
Testing checklist
  1. Unit tests covering logic functions called through the proxy.
  2. Integration tests simulating deploy, initialize, calls, upgrade, and post-upgrade calls.
  3. Negative tests for re-initialization, upgrade failures, and revert paths.
  4. Storage layout comparisons between versions to detect slot shifts.
Audit focus
  • Delegatecall usage and fallback correctness.
  • Storage slot assignments and layout compatibility.
  • Upgrade access controls and initializer protections.
Pro tip
Rehearse upgrades on a staging network and record the exact steps and transactions you will run in production to minimize surprises.

screens.title: Conceptual upgrade exercise
screens.subtitle: Follow the chapter's simulation steps to confirm state preservation

narration.text: This hands-on conceptual exercise walks through the steps described in the chapter without requiring a full toolchain. Step one: design LogicV1 with a public counter, an initialize that sets it, an increment function, and a getVersion returning V1. Step two: design LogicV2 to match storage layout, add a decrement function, and return V2. Step three: deploy LogicV1, then deploy a SimpleProxy pointing at LogicV1. Step four: call initialize through the proxy to set the counter to a known value, then call increment through the proxy to verify the counter increases. Step five: deploy LogicV2, call upgradeTo on the proxy to point to LogicV2, and then call getVersion through the proxy — it should now report V2 while the counter remains preserved. Finally call decrement through the proxy to test the new function. During this exercise pay special attention to two things: ensure LogicV2's state variable declarations match LogicV1's ordering and types, and never call initialize directly on the implementation contract. A common mistake is forgetting to guard initializers; protect them so tests accurately reflect production behavior. This conceptual lab helps internalize the flow and the checks you must run before any real deployment.

keyIdea.title: Exercise goal
keyIdea.text: Simulate deploy, initialize, upgrade, and verify that state persists and new functions behave as expected while maintaining storage compatibility.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Hands-on Exercise
Conceptual Steps to Simulate
  1. Create LogicV1: counter, initialize, increment, getVersion returns V1.
  2. Deploy SimpleProxy pointing at LogicV1 and call initialize through proxy to set counter to 10.
  3. Call increment through proxy and verify counter is 11 via proxy reads.
  4. Deploy LogicV2 with matching storage layout, add decrement and getVersion returns V2.
  5. Call upgradeTo on proxy to point to LogicV2, then verify getVersion returns V2 and counter remains 11. Call decrement and verify counter changes.
Success criteria
State values kept across upgrade; new functions operate as expected; no unexpected overwrites.
Watch out for
Calling initialize on implementation, changing variable order in LogicV2, or leaving upgradeTo unprotected.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Keep these three ideas top-of-mind when working with upgradeable contracts. First, immutability is a security guarantee but it can hinder maintenance; proxies exist to preserve state while allowing logic to evolve. Second, delegatecall is the mechanism that executes implementation code in the proxy's storage context and preserves the original caller, which is both powerful and risky. Third, storage collisions happen when variable order or types change between implementations; they can corrupt proxy-critical data. These ideas are the anchors for safe upgrade design: respect immutability's trade-offs, understand delegatecall semantics precisely, and never change storage layout without careful planning and tooling. Ask yourself: does my project need upgradeability, and if so, have I planned the storage layout and governance controls to make upgrades safe? Key Concepts — Part 1 means upgradeability preserves address and state by using a proxy and delegatecall, but it requires strict storage discipline and secure upgrade governance.. In practical terms, three essential ideas from this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Upgradeability preserves address and state by using a proxy and delegatecall, but it requires strict storage discipline and secure upgrade governance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts
Immutability
Deployed code cannot change; proxies trade some simplicity to allow fixes while preserving state.
Proxy & Implementation
Proxy holds state and forwards execution; implementations are replaceable logic modules.
delegatecall
Runs implementation code in proxy storage and preserves the original caller and value.
Summary
Use proxies to evolve logic when necessary, but enforce storage layout discipline, initializer guards, and strong upgrade governance.

narration.text: These three practice reminders highlight safety controls you should adopt. First, protect the upgrade function with restrictive governance such as a multisig and a delay, because changing implementation is powerful and potentially dangerous. Second, always initialize and exercise logic through the proxy so state is set where it belongs; never treat the implementation as user-facing. Third, adopt testing and auditing practices that include storage-layout checks and upgrade simulations so you catch collisions and initializer bugs before production. Together these habits help you reap the benefits of upgradeability while managing the increased complexity. Before upgrading in production, ask: who can upgrade, how will we test it, and how will users be notified? If you can answer these clearly, your upgrade process will be safer and auditable. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Guard upgrades with multisig/timelock, always interact through the proxy, and run upgrade-specific tests and audits.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Practice Reminders
Governance
Restrict upgrade control with multisig and time delays to reduce centralization risk.
Proxy-first interactions
Always call initialize and other functions through the proxy so state resides in the proxy.
Testing & Audit
Simulate upgrades, check storage layout, and audit delegatecall and fallback behavior.
Final Prompt
Before choosing upgradeability, weigh whether preserving state and address justifies the additional design, testing, and governance burden.
